title: The things we’re secretly scared of when it comes to money
summary: From losing income to sending money to the wrong account, some money worries keep us up at night. Here's how to make them a little less scary.
body_markdown:
It’s 3 am, and the phone is lighting up the ceiling. What if my main client does not renew next month? What if that transfer went to the wrong account number and it has already left? What if the card declines in a city where I know nobody? What if someone at home calls tonight and needs money by morning?


We rarely say these out loud, yet most of us carry some version of them. At that hour, they feel shapeless. In daylight, most turn out to be a few specific risks and a few specific steps.


Five money fears tend to keep people awake: losing income, a payment that never arrives, a transfer sent to the wrong person, running out of money abroad, and an emergency at home. Each is partly rational and partly reducible. Below, we name each one, say what is true in it, and give one step that makes it smaller.


## What if I lose my income?


Of the five, this is the one with the most reason behind it. Clients leave, contracts end, companies restructure, and a salary that felt permanent can stop with a month’s notice. We are not being dramatic when we worry about it.


What we can usually reduce is how fast the fear turns into a crisis. Two numbers do most of the work. The first is the cost of one month: rent, food, transport, data, and any fixed obligations such as school fees or loan repayments. The second is how much of your income comes from one source. If a single client or employer pays most of it, losing them hurts differently from losing one of five.


Always have a buffer of one month’s costs, kept somewhere separate from the account you spend from. One month is not a deep cushion but it’s enough to turn a sudden stop into a few weeks of choices instead of a few days of panic. From there, three months is a common target if you can reach it.


## What if the payment never comes through?


Late payment is perhaps the least troubling of the five, because it does not feel like a disaster. It feels like waiting, refreshing the account, and drafting a polite email for the third time. Invoices do get paid late, and some clients, rather annoyingly, treat the due date, as a suggestion.


Part of the fear can be shrunk before you send an invoice. State the due date and the payment method in writing, and agree what happens if the date passes, such as a late fee or a pause on work. Ask for a deposit on larger jobs so you are never fully exposed. Check that the name on your invoice matches the name on the account that will receive the money. Many banks and payment providers hold a payment for review when the sender's details and the receiving account name do not match, and you may be asked for documents before it is released. A payment can be on its way and still not be spendable.


A follow-up routine helps too: a reminder two days before the due date, one on the day, and one a week later. A scheduled message is easier to send than an anxious one.


## What if I send money to the wrong person?


This is the fear with the sharpest edge, because many transfers cannot simply be taken back. Once a bank transfer has left, getting it returned usually depends on the receiving bank, and on the person who received it, more than on how quickly we notice.


What we can reduce is the chance of it happening, and how fast we act if it does:


- Check the account number, the bank, and the name twice, and read the digits out loud instead of skimming them.
- For a large amount or a new recipient, send a small test first and confirm it arrived before sending the rest.
- Save a recipient only after a transfer has landed with them, so the saved details are the ones that worked.
- If something goes wrong, contact your bank or provider straight away, with the date, amount, reference, and recipient details ready.


Be honest about the odds. Recalls depend on the receiving bank, can carry a fee, and do not always succeed. Speed improves the chances. It does not guarantee a return.


We cannot remove this fear completely, and we should not pretend to. We can make the mistake less likely and the response faster, which is most of what is in our control.


## What if I run out of money abroad?


Being abroad changes the shape of this worry. At home, a failed card is an annoyance. Somewhere else, it can mean a missed ride, a stalled hotel check-in, or a long call to a bank that is closed. Some of the fear is justified: cards do get declined abroad, banks do flag unfamiliar transactions, and the exchange rate at a till can be worse than the one on your phone.


These steps can help:


- Carry a second way to pay that does not depend on the first, ideally from a different provider, and keep it apart from your main card.
- Keep a small amount of cash in the local currency for the first day.
- Keep a buffer in the currency you will be spending, not only in naira, so a swing in the exchange rate does not shrink your trip while you are on it.
- Check what each card charges for payments abroad before you leave, because the fee can differ a lot from one card to another.


The part of this fear that is not rational is the idea that one failed payment means everything has failed. Usually, it means we need the second option, and the point of having one is that the first failure becomes a small event.


## What if there's an emergency back home?


This is the fear that does not stay in our own heads, because it arrives as a phone call and a familiar voice. Money for a hospital deposit or a parent's rent is needed quickly, and to a specific place. An emergency usually comes with a deadline, and the person asking cannot wait for an exchange rate to improve.


What can be decided in advance is the route and the amount. Know how money reaches that person: which bank, which account name, which details, and whether it can arrive at all on a weekend or a public holiday. Ask someone at home to confirm those details now, in a calm moment, and save them. Decide what you can send without breaking your own plans. And keep a buffer for it in the currency you would send from.


Transfer times vary by route and by day, so learn how long your usual route takes before you need it, not on the day. Treat any delivery estimate as an estimate, and leave room around bank cut-off times.


We carry this fear because we care about the people on the other end of it. That is not something to fix. What we can do is make the next call a little less frightening by doing the dull preparation before it comes.


## Frequently asked questions


### Can you reverse a bank transfer sent to the wrong person?


Sometimes, but not always. It depends on the receiving bank, the type of transfer, and whether the money has already been spent. Contact your bank or provider immediately, because speed improves the chances, and expect that a fee may apply.


### What should I do first if I sent money to the wrong account?


Contact your bank or provider straight away. Have the date, amount, transaction reference, and the recipient's details ready, and say what went wrong in plain terms. Do not wait to see whether the recipient notices.


### How big should my emergency fund be if my income is irregular?


Start with one month of essential costs, then build towards three to six months. People with irregular income often aim for the higher end, because a gap can last longer. These are general guidelines, not financial advice.


### Why is my payment pending or on hold?


Providers often hold a payment for verification when the sender's details and the receiving account name do not match, or when more information is needed about the source of the funds. You may be asked for documents before the money is released.


### How do I avoid running out of money when I travel?


Carry two ways to pay from different providers, keep a little cash in the local currency, keep a buffer in the currency you will spend, and check each card's fees for payments abroad before you leave.


### Is it normal to be anxious about money?


Yes. Money worries are common, and some of them are rational. A useful way to handle them is to separate the part that is a real risk from the part that is not, and then act on the part you can change.
